What Happens to Your NFL Bet When a Game Is Postponed, Delayed, or Suspended

Published October 30, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Our guide to NFL push rules covers what happens when a game finishes exactly on the number. This one covers a rarer but far messier situation: a game that doesn't finish on schedule at all. A two-hour lightning delay in Tampa, a hurricane forcing a game to a different city and day, a power outage that stops play mid-third-quarter — these events don't come up often, but when they do, bettors are often surprised to learn that "postponed" and "delayed" aren't settled the same way, and that the rulebook a sportsbook actually follows is buried in house rules most people never read until they need them.

In this guide

  1. The core rule every book leans on
  2. A same-day delay is not the same as a postponement
  3. When a game is stopped after it's already started

The core rule every book leans on

Nearly every regulated U.S. sportsbook's house rules contain some version of the same clause: a wager has "action" only if the game is completed as scheduled, or within a defined grace window if the start or finish gets pushed back. The exact wording varies by operator, but the underlying idea is consistent — a bet is priced on a specific matchup happening at a specific time, and if that matchup doesn't happen within the window the book considers equivalent to "as scheduled," the bet is voided and the stake is returned as no action rather than graded as a win or loss.

That single clause is doing a lot of work. It's the reason a two-hour weather delay almost never affects your ticket, while a game bumped to a different date entirely almost always does. The dividing line is whether the book still considers the game to be the "same event" it opened a line on, and that line is drawn by time elapsed and, in some cases, by whether the starting lineups or site of the game changed materially.

Why this matters more than it seems: the no-action rule isn't a courtesy the book extends to you — it protects the book too. A postponed game often sits for days or weeks with injuries, suspensions, and weather forecasts shifting, and neither side wants to be locked into a price that no longer reflects anything close to the original matchup.

A same-day delay is not the same as a postponement

The NFL has had its share of weather stoppages — lightning in the Gulf Coast and Florida markets most commonly, severe thunderstorms elsewhere, occasionally extreme cold or dangerous travel conditions around the stadium. In the overwhelming majority of these cases, the game is delayed, not postponed: play stops for an hour, two hours, sometimes longer, and then resumes the same day, often with the same network broadcast and the same betting board simply paused. Because the game still happens on its scheduled date between the same two teams, this kind of delay almost never triggers a no-action void. Your pregame spread, total, and moneyline bets stay exactly as they were, and in-play bets simply pick back up once the action does.

A true postponement — moving the game to a different day, and occasionally a different city — is rare in the NFL compared to leagues like MLB, where rainouts are a seasonal fact of life. When it has happened, it's typically been forced by something bigger than ordinary weather: a hurricane threatening a host city, a public health or safety emergency, or infrastructure problems that make the original venue unusable on schedule. In those cases, every operator's house rules point the same direction: pregame straight bets on that game are voided and refunded, full stop, regardless of what the line looked like when you placed it.

When a game is stopped after it's already started

The trickiest scenario is a suspension mid-game — the game has already kicked off, real snaps have been played, and then something stops it before it reaches a natural conclusion. This is genuinely rare in the NFL; the league's venues and scheduling build in enough buffer that games which start are, in practice, almost always finished the same day, even if that means a long weather delay in the middle. But "almost always" isn't "always," and when a suspended game can't be completed and resumed within the operator's defined window, the standard house-rules treatment is to grade the event as no action and void the related bets, exactly as with a full postponement — not to lock in the score at the moment of suspension as if it were a final result.

That last point trips people up. A football score at the moment of a stoppage isn't a reliable proxy for what the final score would have been — unlike, say, a baseball game called in the middle innings, where there's a long tradition of using the score at stoppage as official once a minimum number of innings has been played. The NFL and its betting partners don't have an equivalent "games called" convention, so the default is to treat an incomplete game as exactly that: incomplete, and not a basis for settling a bet either way.

How different bet types are affected

Not every market on a disrupted game gets treated identically, because not every market depends on the game happening on the same date with the same participants.

Bet typeTypical treatment if the game is postponed to a new date
Spread, moneyline, total (pregame)Void, full refund — the game is treated as not played within the betting window
Player props (passing yards, receptions, etc.)Void if that player doesn't ultimately play in the rescheduled game, including if they're injured, rested, or traded before the makeup date
Live/in-play bets already settled on completed segmentsGenerally honored if a clear, independent outcome was already graded before the stoppage (e.g., a first-half total that had already finished); otherwise void
Season-long futures (division winner, win totals)Unaffected — a single game's reschedule doesn't change a season-long market unless it affects the team's remaining schedule in a way the book explicitly addresses

The player-props line is worth sitting with, because it's the case most likely to produce an outcome that feels unfair even though it's consistent with the stated rules. If you bet a running back's rushing yards on a Thursday game that gets postponed to the following Monday, and that back is then ruled out with an unrelated injury suffered in practice before the makeup date, your prop voids — you don't win or lose on a bet that was built around a player who never actually took a snap in the rescheduled game.

What it does to parlays and teasers

If a game on your parlay or teaser gets postponed and voided, the settlement logic is the same remove-and-reprice approach our push rules guide walks through for a pushed leg. A voided leg is treated as no action and dropped from the ticket; the remaining legs are repriced and your ticket continues on just those legs. A five-leg parlay with one postponed game becomes a four-leg parlay priced off the other four games, and if it shrinks all the way down to a single leg, that leg typically pays out as a straight bet at its own odds. The one meaningful difference from a pure push is that a postponement can take days or weeks to resolve — some books will hold the rest of the ticket open and let the other legs settle in real time while the postponed leg's status is pending, rather than freezing the whole ticket until the rescheduled game is played.

Futures, season props, and the bigger picture

It's worth separating single-game disruptions from anything that touches a team's full-season outlook. A game moving from Sunday to the following Wednesday because of a weather emergency doesn't, by itself, change a division-winner future or a season win total — those markets are priced on the full slate of remaining games, and a reschedule within the same season simply shifts when one of those games happens rather than removing it. Where futures can genuinely be affected is the rarer case of a game being canceled outright rather than merely moved, which would actually shorten a team's schedule; operators address that scenario explicitly in their futures house rules, and it's specific enough to each book's terms that it's worth checking directly rather than assuming a universal answer.

What to actually do when it happens to you

If a game you've bet gets delayed, the practical answer in almost every case is to do nothing — the bet is still live and will settle normally once the game resumes and finishes, even if that's hours later than planned. If a game gets fully postponed to a different date, check your account; regulated books generally process the no-action refund automatically once the postponement is confirmed, without you needing to request anything, though the timing can lag a day or two behind the news itself showing up in media coverage. The one time it's worth proactively contacting support is a mid-game suspension that drags on for an unusually long time without a clear resumption plan — that's the scenario most likely to have edge cases in an operator's specific house rules that a general guide like this one can't predict for every book.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to request a refund if my NFL bet is voided by a postponement?

Usually not. Regulated sportsbooks typically process no-action refunds automatically once a postponement is official, crediting your stake back to your account balance without any action on your part, though it can take a little time to post.

If a game is delayed by two hours for weather, does my spread bet change?

No. As long as the game is still played the same day between the same two teams, a weather delay almost never affects pregame bets — the line you locked in stands, and the game simply resumes once conditions allow.

What happens to my player prop if the game moves to a new date and that player later gets hurt in practice?

It's typically voided. Most books only grade a player prop as action if that specific player actually participates in the game as eventually played, so an injury suffered before a rescheduled makeup date generally results in a refund rather than a loss.

Does a postponed game affect a season-long futures bet, like a division winner or win total?

Generally no, as long as the game is rescheduled rather than canceled outright. A reschedule just shifts when a game is played within the season; a true cancellation that shortens the schedule is the scenario that can actually affect a futures market, and that's addressed in each book's specific futures house rules.

Is a suspended game ever graded using the score at the moment play stopped?

Not under standard NFL betting house rules. Unlike some sports with long-standing conventions for calling a contest official after a minimum amount of play, football betting markets generally treat an unfinished game as incomplete and void the related bets rather than locking in a mid-game score as final.
